system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2125-02-01 18:12:00 to 2125-02-05 17:35:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, gastroparesis, and chronic back pain was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and severe back pain similar to prior episodes. She presented with hyperglycemia but no ketoacidosis and was managed with IV fluids, antiemetics, and pain control. Her symptoms were inconsistent and closely tied to anxiety and emotional distress. Despite extensive prior workup showing only gastritis and H. pylori, her symptoms recurred, often near discharge. Psychiatric evaluation revealed that depression and anxiety were major barriers to outpatient care adherence. She improved with supportive care, was weaned off IV medications, and tolerated a full diet. Due to the psychosocial component of her recurrent admissions, she was transitioned to a crisis center for voluntary psychiatric admission. Her insulin was adjusted to 28 units of Lantus nightly, and she was discharged on oral tramadol, continued metoclopramide, and omeprazole, with follow-up planned for H. pylori treatment and physical therapy.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Major depressive affective disorder, single episode, unspecified
Diabetes with renal manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Diabetes with other specified manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Nephritis and nephropathy, not specified as acute or chronic, in diseases classified elsewhere
Personal history of noncompliance with medical treatment, presenting hazards to health
Other nonspecific findings on examination of urine
Unspecified gastritis and gastroduodenitis, without mention of hemorrhage

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. My blood sugar was 400 this morning, and I’ve been nauseous, throwing up, and my back’s been hurting more than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have type 1 diabetes, correct? And you’ve been taking your insulin as prescribed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been taking my Lantus at night and Humalog with meals. I haven’t missed any doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. You mentioned nausea and vomiting—any fever, chills, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chills. I’ve had more bowel movements—three today—but not watery. Just not feeling hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And your back pain—has it changed recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same as always—low back, doesn’t shoot down. I usually take my mom’s Percocet when it’s bad, but I don’t have any now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ll manage your pain here with safer options. Your blood work shows high glucose, ketones in your urine, and some acidosis—this suggests diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: DKA again? But I took my insulin. Why is this happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes even with proper insulin, stress—like pain or illness—can push your body into DKA. We’ll start an IV insulin drip and fluids to correct this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be in the ICU?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at least for the first 24 hours, so we can monitor you closely. Once your levels stabilize, we’ll move you to the regular floor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is coming down—now 220—and your acid levels are improving. We’re transitioning you off the insulin drip and back to your usual Lantus and Humalog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat something? I’m really hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on a light diet. We also want to treat your nausea—so you’ll continue metoclopramide before meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that before. Does it help with gastroparesis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help with delayed stomach emptying. But your prior tests showed normal emptying, so we think your nausea is more related to DKA and possibly stomach inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Inflammation? Like from that H. pylori infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re restarting treatment for H. pylori with two antibiotics and a stronger acid blocker for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that last time. Do I really need it again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because if it’s not fully treated, it can keep causing stomach irritation and make diabetes harder to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team came by. They recommend starting acetaminophen and tramadol for your back pain, and a lidocaine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No stronger painkillers? I usually need something more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, we’re being cautious with opioids. These medications are safer and should help, especially with physical therapy later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess. But my back pain makes my blood sugar go up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s true—pain and stress do raise blood sugar. Managing your pain well will help your diabetes too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking much better. Blood sugar is stable, and your kidney function has improved. We’re planning to move you out of the ICU today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re doing well. Your vitals are stable, and you’re eating without vomiting. We just need to make sure your insulin doses keep your sugars in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still worried I’ll end up back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we’re setting up visiting nurses to help you at home with insulin and blood sugar checks twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s helpful. What about my mental health? I’ve been feeling really down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry recommended continuing your sertraline and adding outpatient therapy. They also suggested psychiatric visiting nurses to check in weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t like the last crisis center. It felt scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You won’t be going back there. This is about support at home—helping you stay on track with both your physical and mental health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood work this morning is excellent. Glucose is 90, no ketones, and your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you keep doing this well. We’ll finalize your discharge plan today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue 28 units of Lantus at night, Humalog with meals, and the new H. pylori treatment for 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The antibiotics and Protonix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—amoxicillin, levofloxacin, and pantoprazole. It’s important to finish all of them, even if you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tramadol every 4 hours as needed, acetaminophen every 8 hours, and the lidocaine patch daily. And please follow up with physical therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged for home health to visit twice daily for insulin education and blood sugar monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I sometimes get confused with the sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’ll help you feel more confident. Also, GI wants to see you in two weeks to check on your stomach treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my primary doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with them in one week. They’ll coordinate your diabetes, back pain, and mental health care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’ve done really well—your labs are normal, and you’re eating and moving well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m nervous, but I’ll try to stick to the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. Call your doctor if your blood sugar goes above 300 or below 70, or if you start vomiting again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my back pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try the tramadol and acetaminophen first. If it doesn’t help, or if you have numbness or weakness, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I still check my blood sugar four times a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with the sliding scale insulin. The visiting nurses will help you review the logs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And no alcohol with the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly—avoid alcohol while on levofloxacin and for a few days after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing all the right things. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. The discharge nurse will go over your meds and paperwork now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes and a history of recurrent DKA was admitted for hyperglycemia, nausea, vomiting, and chronic back pain. She was diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis and managed in the ICU with an insulin drip and fluid resuscitation. Her condition improved with transition to subcutaneous insulin, and she was moved to the medical floor. Treatment included restarting H. pylori therapy for gastritis, managing nausea with metoclopramide, and addressing back pain with acetaminophen, tramadol, and a lidocaine patch. Psychiatric comorbidities were acknowledged, and a plan for outpatient mental health support and visiting nurses was established. She was discharged home with services, on stable insulin therapy, antibiotics, and pain management, with follow-up arranged for diabetes, GI, and physical therapy.
